#6533. At the Races: After the deluge

Tuesday’s rout by Democrats has led one group dedicated to electing more Republican women to Congress to warn of a “crisis-level decline” of female GOP members on Capitol Hill.

Danielle Barrow, the president of Women for Women Action Fund, drew parallels between this week’s results and the 2018 blue wave.

“After 2018, when Republicans lost 40 seats and elected only one new Republican woman, the party made a real commitment to recruiting and investing in women – and it worked,” Barrow said in a statement Wednesday, adding that women accounted for 11 of the 15 House seats the GOP picked up in the 2020 election. But she cautioned that the party needs to sustain that focus across election cycles.

“Republicans cannot only make this investment after a wipeout election and abandon it when things improve,” she said. “It is time for party leaders to treat this as a permanent strategy, not a crisis response.”

The ranks of House Republican women won’t plummet to as low as after the 2018 elections, when the caucus had just 13 female members. At least 18 Republican women have won House races so far, according to The Associated Press, and two others are leading as of Thursday afternoon. The conference is likely to see two new female members: Florida’s Sydney Gruters, the wife of RNC Chairman Joe Gruters, and Washington state’s Amanda McKinney, who holds a comfortable lead as votes continue to be counted.

Still, those figures are worlds apart from House Democrats, whose caucus will have more than 100 women next year.

“We have always known that when women run, women win,” Florida Rep. Lois Frankel, chair of the member-led Elect Democratic Women PAC, said in a statement Wednesday.

Those incoming new members span the ideological range of the party, including progressives from New York and California who scored big primary wins this summer, to more moderate Democrats who flipped seats in Virginia and Pennsylvania.

House Democrats had set a public goal this cycle to push their female membership past 100. Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who is retiring at the end of the year, said electing Democratic women had been her “passion” since she joined the House in 1987.

“We made a decision to make more room for women at the tables of power – and generations of candidates, organizers and supporters have carried that work forward,” she said.

Blue breakthrough: Democrats flipped the House and Senate this week, giving the party one of its biggest nights in decades. On the Senate side, they wrested seats from Republicans in Texas, South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina and Ohio, while finally flipping Maine. Meanwhile, on the House side, Democrats were on track to not just win every race rated a Toss-up by Inside Elections but also pick up seats in deep-red territory that weren’t considered competitive until late in the cycle. Mary Ellen and Daniela summed up their initial election night takeaways, including how Democratic moderates and progressives both cheered the results and why many of Trump’s picks flopped at the ballot box.

Not going anywhere: The top Senate Democrat, Charles E. Schumer of New York, is confident he will be elected majority leader by his caucus, especially after the party’s resounding midterm wins. Several of his incoming members have promised to support others, our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports, but the reality is there’s no real plausible alternative. Schumer’s own seat is up in 2028.

Redistricting rout: Republicans’ redistricting gambit hasn’t paid off as they’d hoped, the latest election results show, with the GOP appearing poised to flip only a handful of redrawn seats. Democratic incumbents who sought reelection from their reconfigured seats appeared poised to all win, although the race for Rep. Darren Soto’s Central Florida seat remained uncalled as of Thursday afternoon.

Taking the chair: Among the bruising defeats that North Carolina Republicans suffered this week was National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson’s loss to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator. Hudson is now the second party campaign chief to lose reelection this decade after New York’s Sean Patrick Maloney , who lost in 2022 while serving as the DCCC chair.

New senators: The incoming Senate Democratic class includes a returning senator, a former governor, two lieutenant governors and a congressman, a notable amount of governing experience. Meanwhile, five Republican House members are moving across the Rotunda after winning open Senate seats.

Member-to-governor pipeline grows: Five newly elected governors will be departing Capitol Hill to become the top executive of their state or territory, Savannah reports. Additionally, two former members who also served in the Biden administration were elected governor, though a trio of House Republicans fell short in their gubernatorial bids.

Comeback season: Roll Call’s Nick Eskow reports on the former members who are poised to return to the House or Senate next year, with at least seven winning comeback bids Tuesday.

The firsts: Several candidates made history this week with their elections to Congress or the governorships of their state. Roll Call’s Andrew Menezes rounds up the milestone wins.

D.C. in the House: Robert White, D.C.’s newly elected nonvoting delegate, told our colleague Nina Heller that he plans to lobby fellow Democrats next year to support D.C. statehood. A potential selling point: The party could tackle affordability concerns better with two Democratic senators from the deep-blue District, he said.

Keeping count: As of 4:30 p.m. Thursday, Democrats had flipped 42 seats in the House and seven in the Senate, according to the AP. Republicans have so far picked up two House seats, both through redistricting. Twenty-eight House contests and two Senate races (Alaska and Mississippi) remain uncalled as of publication time. Check out Roll Call’s results tracker for updates as the races are called.

Indie losses: Independent Senate hopefuls running in deep-red states did not find success on Tuesday, even in races without a Democrat on the ballot. In Nebraska, former union leader Dan Osborn came up short in his second Senate bid. In Idaho, former state legislator Todd Achilles failed to dislodge Sen. Jim Risch, while Navy veteran Brian Bengs couldn’t topple South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds. In Montana, where the Democratic nominee did not drop out, former university president Seth Bodnar lost to Republican Kurt Alme. On the House side, Alaska GOP Rep. Nick Begich comfortably leads commercial fisherman Bill Hill, though below the 50 percent threshold needed to avoid a ranked-choice runoff. With votes still being counted, the AP had yet to call the race at publication time.

Not just Congress: The blue wave that broke Republican majorities on Capitol Hill also washed over state legislatures. Democrats are poised to hold new majorities in 12 legislative chambers, including the North Carolina House and Texas House, according to the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, although some results aren’t official yet. The party also won governing trifectas in Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Meanwhile, in blue states, Democrats tightened their grip on government: In Rhode Island, Republicans are on track to hold just 10 seats in the entire 113-member legislature, while next door in Connecticut, the 36-seat Senate could have as few as three GOP members.

Blame game: As Republicans take stock of what went wrong for them in the midterms, Vice President JD Vance was quick to point to the Iran conflict as an insurmountable albatross. “The reason we lost is the war,” Vance said in a lengthy X post. “If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. … But everyone knows why we lost.”

But the tariffs: A pair of Republican former senators, Arizona’s Jeff Flake and Pennsylvania’s Patrick J. Toomey, both also urged their party to focus on the impact of Trump’s tariff policies. “Arbitrary and capricious tariffs directly raised costs for all American consumers,” Toomey wrote Wednesday on X. “Many voted for Democrats yesterday.”

Staying put: Pennsylvania Rep. Brendan F. Boyle says he will remain in the House, where he’s poised to become the next Budget Committee chair, rather than launch a Democratic primary challenge to Sen. John Fetterman next cycle.

Bayh Bayh Bayh: A third generation of Indiana’s famed Bayh family won political office this week, with Beau Bayh’s election as secretary of state. Bayh, a Marine Corps veteran, follows in the footsteps of his father, Evan Bayh, who won the same post 40 years ago before going on to serve as governor and senator, and his late grandfather, Birch Bayh, who won three terms in the Senate. Indiana Democrats had a breakthrough election this week, defeating GOP Rep. Victoria Spartz, winning a second statewide office, unseating the speaker and breaking the GOP supermajority in the state House.

A win and a loss: Nebraska Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts won reelection, but his wife, Democrat Susanne Shore, lost a special election for a seat on University of Nebraska Board of Regents, which governs the university system. Shore, who lost to a fellow Democrat in the officially nonpartisan race, was making her first bid for elective office.

Bans on the ballot: Voters in Arizona, Nebraska and Washington state have approved new measures barring transgender athletes from participating in girls sports. A similar proposal in Colorado also appears likely to pass, although the AP had yet to call it as of publication time.

Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections shares 15 initial lessons from the midterm elections, from the president’s “political mortality” to candidate quality and the power of personal brands. And, Nathan writes, as bad a night as it was for Republicans, it could have been even worse.

As Maine goes: The New York Times caught up with with Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her bid for a sixth term in Maine. Collins, who had survived tough cycles before, spoke of getting “caught up in the Trump tsunami” and how she finally had her “Margaret Chase Smith moment.”

“These are extinction-level numbers”: Texas Monthly sat down for an interview with former state House Speaker Dade Phelan, who anticipated a down-ballot GOP rout but not the full extent of it. “MAGA needs to be dead,’’ said the Republican, who led the push to impeach state Attorney General Ken Paxton in 2023 and then was targeted for defeat by Trump. He opted against reelection this year.

Corruption a top issue: The Associated Press reported that its 2026 voter poll found corruption at the top of the list of concerns for voters who helped sweep Democrats into power on Capitol Hill.

Tar Heeled: Among the states where Republicans suffered their biggest defeats Tuesday, perhaps none was more stunning than North Carolina, where they've so far lost five U.S. House seats and are trailing in one another and lost control of the state House. The (Raleigh) News & Observer looks at how maps “designed to deliver strong Republican majorities [failed] so spectacularly at that goal.”

Support and discord: Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed’s sharply critical views toward Israel roiled the Jewish community in Michigan. But exit polling suggests most Jewish voters backed him, albeit in smaller numbers than they might have had a different Democrat run, Religion News Service reports.

That's how many House districts won by Trump in 2024 have been called for Democratic candidates by the AP as of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time on Thursday.

Twenty-eight additional Trump-won districts remain uncalled at publication time, and Democrats are currently leading in eight of those races.

The figures stand in sharp contrast to the start of the cycle, when there were just 13 House Democrats in districts that backed Trump in 2024.

Since then, several Republican-led states redrew their congressional maps in an effort to increase the number of Trump-won districts and improve their party’s chances of holding the House.

In large part, this effort appears to have backfired in 2026, with the Democratic wave cresting high enough to wash over dozens of Trump-won districts. Twenty-one of the 52 Democratic wins so far have come in states that redrew their congressional lines: Texas (six Trump-won seats), North Carolina (six), Ohio (five), Florida (three) and Alabama (one).

Congressional Republicans are holding leadership elections next week as they transition from the majority to the minority party. Speaker Mike Johnson is not seeking his conference’s top post, setting up a clash to be the next House minority leader. On the Senate side, South Dakota’s John Thune hopes to continue leading his party in the chamber.

#6532. The Sky This Week from November 20 to 27: Uranus at opposition

Friday, November 20The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M. EST, then passes 7° north of Saturn at 8 P.M. EST. They remain visible all evening, forming a triangle in southern Pisces and northern Cetus. The Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, but Neptune will be invisible without binoculars or a telescope. Check out last week’s column for more details on how to view the celestial trio.

In the northeast, Auriga the Charioteer is above the horizon by 7 P.M. local time. Its brightest star is Capella, which shines at magnitude 0.1 and sits some 43 light-years away. Just southeast of this star, you’ll find another triangle in the sky tonight. This small shape is an asterism about 2.7° long, known as the Kids. It consists of Epsilon (ε), Zeta (ζ), and Eta (η) Aurigae, which range from 3rd (Epsilon and Eta) to 4th (Zeta) magnitude.

Why are these called the Kids? Capella’s name essentially means “She-Goat,” according to the late stellar expert Jim Kaler. These fainter stars cluster close by the brighter star like goat kids around their mother.

Mercury reaches greatest western elongation (20°) at 7 P.M. EST; it will be visible before dawn tomorrow morning, so keep reading for more details.

Sunrise: 6:51 A.M. Sunset: 4:40 P.M. Moonrise: 2:04 P.M. Moonset: 2:12 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (84%) *Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Saturday, November 21If you’ve got a viewing site with a clear eastern horizon, this morning offers a great opportunity to spot the solar system’s innermost planet. Look for Mercury about an hour before sunrise, when it reaches 7° high and shines at magnitude –0.5. The planet reached its greatest western elongation from our Sun yesterday evening, and is now 20° west of our star in the sky.

Located in Libra, the tiny world sits to the far lower left of bright Venus, higher in the sky. Venus is in the constellation Virgo, standing just north (to the upper left) of the bright star Spica. Another bright star, Arcturus in Boötes, hangs to that pair’s far upper left.

Pull out a telescope to check out the size and phase of each planet. Start with Venus, whose disk spans a hefty 46” — currently larger than Jupiter’s apparent size in our sky. Despite its impressive width, however, the disk of Venus appears as just a sliver, only 19% lit. Slide down to Mercury for comparison, and see that its phase is much larger — 62% — while the planet’s overall apparent width is much smaller, just 7”.

If you’re able, keep watching Mercury day by day in the morning sky. Its gibbous phase will continue growing, reaching 84% lit by the end of the month.

Sunrise: 6:52 A.M. Sunset: 4:39 P.M. Moonrise: 2:29 P.M. Moonset: 3:22 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (92%)

Sunday, November 22With the Moon not far from Full, its western limb is now coming into view as the Sun rises across the lunar landscape. The large, flat-floored crater Schickard is prominent in the southwest, near the small, circular Mare Humorum. Because the nearly Full Moon is so bright, you may want to use a Moon filter before you turn your telescope toward our satellite tonight for a closer look.

Zoom in on Schickard to discover that its dark floor isn’t perfectly smooth, but pockmarked by smaller craters that came after the initial, larger crater’s formation. Its outer walls are shallow and beaten down, also showing off their age. Look closely at Schickard’s western wall to see how it has slumped, particularly compared to the eastern side of the crater rim. Also compare the texture of the southwestern portion of the crater floor, which appears quite rough, to the rest of the crater, which is smoother. The difference arises because most of the crater was flooded by lava, which didn’t quite reach its southwestern regions.

Stretching about 130 miles (210 kilometers) across, Schickard is roughly 4 billion years old and was formed by a giant impact. Because it sits so near the limb of the Moon, it often looks oblong from our vantage point on Earth — but from above, orbiters have shown it is really quite circular in shape.

Sunrise: 6:53 A.M. Sunset: 4:39 P.M. Moonrise: 2:59 P.M. Moonset: 4:34 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (97%)

Monday, November 23A few hours after sunset, the house-shaped constellation Cepheus stands on the point of its roof in the northern sky, above the Little Dipper. Cepheus is home to several lovely double stars, including Xi (ξ) Cephei, also known as Kurhah.

Glowing at magnitude 4.3, Kurhah is not one of the stars in the house’s outline, but lies within the boxy base. You can find it about midway between Alderamin (Alpha [α] Cep) and Iota (ι) Cep, the western and eastern points in the house’s box, respectively. Kurhah’s two components are separated by just under 8” — once you find the star in binoculars or your finder scope, any telescope will split them. The pair consists of a brighter magnitude 4.4 primary, which glows white, and a fainter magnitude 6.5 secondary, which appears to many observers as yellow.

If you happen to have a large telescope, you may want to give a nearby deep-sky treasure a try: planetary nebula NGC 7139 sits just 2° west-southwest of Kurhah, but it requires a large scope (8 inches at least) to spot, as this bubble of gas glows at magnitude 13.3. If available, an Oxygen-III filter will help bring it out by dimming the nearby stars.

Sunrise: 6:54 A.M. Sunset: 4:38 P.M. Moonrise: 3:37 P.M. Moonset: 5:52 A.M. Moon Phase: Full

Tuesday, November 24Full Moon occurs at 9:54 A.M. EST, bringing us our second Super Moon of the year. A Super Moon occurs when the Moon reaches Full phase close to perigee, its closest point to Earth, making our satellite appear larger and brighter than average. The November Full Moon is also called the Beaver Moon.

A few hours earlier, before dawn, the Full Moon passes through the Pleiades star cluster (M45) in Taurus, occulting several of its bright stars. This is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope (just note that you may want a Moon filter if available, as our satellite is so big and bright). The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.

The 5th-magnitude star Celaeno (16 Tauri) disappears behind the Moon’s leading edge just moments before 6 A.M. CST, followed minutes later by 4th-magnitude Taygeta (19 Tau). Next to vanish is 4th-magnitude Maia (20 Tau) just before 6:20 A.M. CST, followed quickly by Sterope (21 Tau) a few minutes later. The latter two may be difficult to catch from the Midwest without optical aid, as sunrise is fast approaching. If you are using binoculars or a telescope in this region, make sure to put them away several minutes ahead of sunrise from your location. Celaeno reappears around 6:40 A.M. CST, 15 minutes or so before sunrise.

For specific timings from your location, visit the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

The Moon then passes 5° north of Uranus (also in Taurus) at 2 P.M. EST. Over in the constellation Leo, Mars passes 1.8° north of Regulus at 5 P.M. EST.

Sunrise: 6:55 A.M. Sunset: 4:38 P.M. Moonrise: 4:24 P.M. Moonset: 7:10 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (99%)

Wednesday, November 25The Moon reaches perigee, the closest point to Earth in its orbit, at 4:01 P.M. EST. At that time, our satellite will stand 223,288 miles (359,347 km) away.

The distant ice giant Uranus reaches opposition tonight at 6 P.M. EST. Opposition is the best time to view a planet in our sky, and it’s visible roughly from dusk until dawn. Because Uranus is faint — magnitude 5.6 — you’ll want to give it a few hours after sunset to climb away from both light pollution and turbulent air near the horizon. Around 10 P.M. local time, you’ll find Uranus midway between the bright star Aldebaran and the Pleiades star cluster in Taurus the Bull, about 60° above the southeastern horizon. It sits some 1.5° south of 4th-magnitude 37 Tauri.

Although Uranus can be visible to the naked eye under clear, dark conditions, the bright waning Moon is nearby, so pull out binoculars or a telescope to view the far-off planet tonight. Once you land on its location, look for a “flat,” grayish-colored star. Uranus’ disk spans 4”, so you will likely be able to tell it is circular, rather than a pinpoint of light like any background stars.

Sunrise: 6:56 A.M. Sunset: 4:37 P.M. Moonrise: 5:24 P.M. Moonset: 8:26 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (96%)

Thursday, November 26Celebrate Thanksgiving with a celestial turkey: The famous Orion Nebula (M42) is also playfully known as the Turkey Nebula because it looks to some like a turkey, particularly in deep astrophotos. But whether you’re a photographer or not, this bright deep-sky treat is easy to enjoy tonight while dinner digests.

By about 9 P.M. local time, Orion the Hunter has risen above the eastern horizon, his recognizable three-star belt standing in a vertical line. The lowest star in that line is Alnitak (Zeta [ζ] Orionis), and the Orion Nebula lies just 3.7° south-southwest of this star, to its lower right on the sky this evening. You might be able to spot its glow without optical aid, although the bright Moon nearby may make that difficult. Binoculars or any telescope will easily show it.

At 4th magnitude and spanning some 85’ by 60’, the Orion Nebula is a huge and bright star-forming region that sits roughly 1,350 light-years from Earth. In the brightest portion of the nebula lies a small grouping of young stars called the Trapezium Cluster. Take your time with this gorgeous sight, scanning around the region to pick out detail in the nebulosity. And if you are an astrophotographer, consider turning the view into a Thanksgiving memory to share for years to come.

Sunrise: 6:58 A.M. Sunset: 4:37 P.M. Moonrise: 6:35 P.M. Moonset: 9:33 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (91%)

Friday, November 27The Moon-free window for observing Comet 161P/Hartley-IRAS reopens tonight, the same day the comet reaches perihelion, the closest point to the Sun in its 21½-year orbit. It has been a fairly stable 10th to 11th magnitude, and although it has no appreciable tail, the nucleus’ green glow has been notable in recent astrophotos.

You’ll find Hartley-IRAS in the west a few hours after sunset. Around 7 P.M. local time it is still 30° high, well above the turbulent air near the ground that can muddy astronomical views. Tonight the comet is in western Sagitta, about 6.3° north-northeast of 3rd-magnitude Zeta (ζ) Aquilae. Even a small (4-inch) scope will net you a view, but larger apertures will show more detail around the nucleus, allowing you to look for features such as a sharpened southern flank as it flies into the solar headwind.

While you’re in this region, make sure to sweep just 2.1° northeast of the comet’s location to spot the famous Coathanger asterism in Vulpecula. This 1°-long grouping of stars looks just like its namesake, with the hook on the southern side of the hanger’s arms.

Sunrise: 6:59 A.M. Sunset: 4:36 P.M. Moonrise: 7:53 P.M. Moonset: 10:26 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (82%)

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

#6531. 18 Family Resorts That Go Above and Beyond for Those With Babies and Toddlers

I've traveled to some pretty far-flung places, but nothing could have prepared me for the logistical circus of vacationing with a baby. Four years and 30 countries later, my son Julian has taught me a thing or two about what makes a resort genuinely welcoming to its littlest guests. For starters, there’s a massive difference between a hotel that hands your kid a coloring book at check-in and one that has anticipated the thousands of little things that can make or break a family vacation.

The best resorts for infants and toddlers also understand that keeping littles happy isn’t a one-size-fits-all proposition. A baby might need a quiet nursery and a reliable nanny; a three-year-old might be thrilled to feed goats on an Austrian farm, explore a Japanese forest, or make plaster casts of lion tracks in the Kalahari. And parents? Sometimes we just want to eat dinner without having to negotiate with a tiny inquisitor.

That kind of thoughtfulness is what sets the properties on this list apart. I’ve seen it firsthand at more than half a dozen of them, where the greatest luxury wasn’t necessarily the thread count or the size of the swimming pool, but getting to enjoy a five-star vacation instead of merely financing one for your offspring. Read on for the best resorts for infants and toddlers.

Location: Savusavu, FijiPrice: From $1,136 per night

Jet lag aside, this is one of the rare luxury resorts where traveling with a child feels not just doable, but deeply supported. Every family with a child under five is assigned two dedicated nannies—one for daytime adventures, one for evenings—so parents can book a snorkeling trip with the resident marine biologist or linger over a blissfully kid-free dinner. When my son and I arrived in 2024—the first international stop on our 88-day, 14-country trip—it took me all of four minutes to abandon any guilt I had about dropping him off. His nanny was warm, attentive, and completely unfazed by toddlers being toddlers; she whisked him away for glass-bottom boat rides, hermit crab hunts, and splashes in the resort’s “mushroom-cascade” wading pool.

Parents of even younger children will appreciate the made-to-order purées and unlimited milk supply; nurseries stocked with infant cots, toys, and baby baths; and daily laundry service and disposable diapers for sale in the on-site boutique. Following a spring 2026 renovation, the resort now has five two-bedroom bures (a traditional Fijian hut or cabin), giving families more room to spread out. The Bula Club—essentially a resort within a resort—has a sun-safe junior pool with a waterslide, trampoline, and tricycles.

Location: Flamands Beach, St. BartsPrice: From $805 per night

With 61 rooms, suites, and villas, Cheval Blanc is one of the glammest maisons on an island full of glammy maisons. The inn has even partnered with high-end Parisian baby accessories brand Baudou to spoil its style-conscious guests. Cots are dressed in the finest linens, and rooms include a changing table with a diaper basket and baby care products, a rattan high chair with a cushioned seat, baby-friendly crockery, and a hand-stitched bib embroidered with seahorses and stars. Wee beach towels and a selection of beach toys are available for afternoon romps on Flamands, one of the prettiest powder-white beaches in St. Barts. At the new Le Carrousel play space, children ages 3 to 12 can climb aboard an imaginary exploration vessel, tumble into a coconut-themed ball pit, and discover the island’s Arawak history through interactive storytelling. Come mealtime, they can indulge in made-to-order baby purées prepared by the in-house culinary team. Upon request, a professional photographer can be brought to the premises to document your family trip.

Location: West End, AnguillaPrice: From $725 per night

Toddlers are greeted with custom Anguilla-themed stuffies, pint-sized bathrobes, and slippers at this upscale resort on Anguilla’s West End, where accommodations range from contemporary-chic guest rooms to five-bedroom beachfront villas, some with private pools and kitchens. Wherever you rest your head, expect kids to squeal when they catch a glimpse of the iguanas that freely roam the property. The zero-entry Bamboo Pool has mini loungers for infants; other five-star amenities include complimentary cribs, strollers, car seats, bottle sterilizers, baby tubs, Le Petit Prince toiletries, SlumberPods, and organic puréed baby food on the room service menu. A refreshed splash pad offers another place for little ones to cool off, while children five and under eat free from the kids menu throughout the resort. Also notable: American Airlines operates year-round nonstop flights from Miami, while AnguillAir offers seasonal service from Boston, Newark, and Baltimore, so families no longer have to hitch a ride over from St. Maarten.

Location: Karatu, TanzaniaPrice: From $518 per adult per night, including full board

After a long-haul flight with a toddler, Gibb’s Farm feels like an exhale. Set on 80 acres of organic gardens and coffee groves on the forested outer slopes of the Ngorongoro Crater, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, the property is an ideal place to begin or end a safari. My son was only 20 months old when we stayed here, but we happily spent hours roaming the gardens, chasing chickens, and learning how to milk cows. The farm’s one-bedroom cottages—many decorated with pieces from Gibb’s unique artist-in-residence program—are ideal for families, offering private terraces, outdoor showers, and enough breathing room for mid-tantrum resets.

There’s no kids club, but toddlers are warmly embraced here. The staff arranged a private game drive for us so we could move at Julian’s pace, stopping for snack breaks and diaper changes as needed. In the crater—home to one of the densest populations of large mammals in Africa—we saw lions, hippos, warthogs, wildebeest, and flamingos, but it was the dazzle of zebras milling around our vehicle that most delighted my son. Back on the farm, little ones can collect eggs, feed the pigs, wander among the coffee shrubs, splash in the pool, or learn about the music and customs of the local Iraqw tribe through hands-on cultural activities.

Location: Palm Beach, FloridaPrice: From $890 per night

Florida is a perennially popular destination for young families, and no resort rolls out the red carpet for babies better than the Breakers Palm Beach. Founded in 1896, the luxury hotel has a private beach and four oceanfront pools, including a zero-entry one designed specifically for youngsters. There’s also a 4,500-square-foot playground with slides, tunnels, and bridges, plus the new Seaside Family Entertainment Center, a beachfront hub with a dedicated Toddler Cove, arts and crafts, and interactive games. Cribs, infant baths, bottle warmers, and strollers are available upon request, as is the childproofing of guest rooms, which involves padding perilously edged furniture, covering electrical sockets, and removing trash bags from cans. Bicycles with baby seats and children’s bikes are available to rent, as are private poolside bungalows with a dedicated concierge standing by, ready to fetch popsicles and pool toys at a moment’s notice. Other big wins for tiny visitors: poolside spin art, Build-A-Bear workshops, and daily children’s programming.

Location: Punta Cana, Dominican RepublicPrice: From $850 per night

For parents seeking a more home-like environment, the multi-bedroom villas at this secluded Relais & Chateaux property offer spacious living rooms, full kitchens, and private pools. Staff arrange scavenger hunts and arts and crafts hours; for an additional $325, parents can reserve the VIBabies package. This comes with two hours of complimentary babysitting plus a host of handy gear—including a portable crib (with turndown service!), a changing table, diapers, a bottle warmer, a baby monitor, an infant tub, pool alarms, a Baby Einstein play table, a 4moms MamaRoo baby swing, and a basket of kid-approved snacks and juices. For fun in the sun, Eden Roc will throw in a pop-up beach playpen, swim nappies, and sun protection gear (a bucket hat, colored sunglasses, Nivea sun lotion, and aloe vera gel) for use at the sandy beach and artificial lagoon.

Location: Nuevo Nayarit, MexicoPrice: From $454 per adult per night

Families vacationing at this AAA Five Diamond resort on the Riviera Nayarit are assigned a baby concierge who coordinates all meals and nanny services. Whatever gear you don’t want to drag from home—crib, stroller, baby tub and toiletries, bottle brush and sterilizer, pacifier, floaties—the team can arrange for on-site, all complimentary. Parents checking in with infants also receive a sleep guide developed with pediatric sleep consultant Rachael Shepard-Ohta of Hey Sleepy Baby, with tips for managing time zone changes and maintaining bedtime routines on the road. The kids club is stocked with books, blocks, and a play kitchen; parents may additionally request a crib mobile, rattle, or teether for use in the room.

Some suites have private plunge pools, but the hotel jewel is the triple-tiered, multi-temperature infinity pool. Mini cabanas await down at the beach, along with hooded baby towels and fresh-squeezed juice. Young spa-goers can opt for a gentle sunrise massage soundtracked by Mozart or a chocolate explosion face mask, then strike a pose with mom or dad during a baby yoga class. Executive chef Guillaume Morancé and his team prepare gourmet purées to challenge young palates (think white fish with celery, leeks, and mushroom) at every meal. The resort even offers a Mi Primer Fiesta package for celebrating a baby's first birthday, complete with piñatas and foam.

Location: Koh Yao Yai, ThailandPrice: From $308 per night

Set on one of the Andaman’s last unspoiled islands—reachable only by boat and blissfully free of traffic—this resort feels worlds away from the party throngs on Phuket and Krabi. When Julian and I visited in 2024, it was during a vintage sidecar tour through rubber plantations and rice fields that I realized how special this island really is: no honking, no rush, just villagers waving as you pass. The accommodations were a slam dunk too: Family suites with bunk beds and tipi play tents come stocked with baby tubs, bottle warmers, sterilizers, baby chairs, and toys. The Grand Family Suite ups the ante with a chocolate treasure box at check-in, while all families with children receive a treasure map. Ground-floor suites open directly onto the resort’s enormous family pool, while infants and early swimmers have dedicated splash zones and shallow areas. As a bonus, the staff truly adores kids—one affable pool attendant peeled off his socks and shoes and joined my son on the slides when he saw how happy it made him.

Pristine beach and pools aside, the resort is home to southern Thailand’s largest kids club, featuring climbing walls, a dance stage, and an epic ball pit. Parents can join kids under six for Junior Explorer activities like kite making, batik painting, and sandcastle building, or arrange a family excursion to go island-hopping by longtail boat. For something even more tailored, little ones can try Muay Thai lessons, aerial yoga, or beach fishing with locals.

Location: Beaver Creek, ColoradoPrice: From $275 per night

Ask anyone who has ever attempted skiing with a toddler—it takes an act of Congress just to get them into a snowsuit. What saved my sanity at Park Hyatt Beaver Creek was that the slopes were, quite literally, outside our front door. This 189-room, chateau-style property is one of only two true ski-in, ski-out hotels at the base of Beaver Creek Mountain Resort, and that convenience is priceless. I could bundle up my kiddo and hand him off to a private instructor at the Ski and Snowboard School (open to ages three and up) and know that he was in eternally patient hands. After his post-lesson hot chocolates, Julian burned off whatever energy he had left in the family game room and the snowy outdoor playground before splashing around in the heated pool and hot tubs—his preferred après.

Location: Palm Desert, CaliforniaPrice: From $348 per night, including a $45 daily resort fee

This 450-acre resort features a 12,000-square-foot arcade—the largest hotel arcade in California. This is great news for kids of all ages who are stoked to play retro video games, test their skills in high-tech simulators, or try their hand at duckpin bowling. Family by JW programming gets the whole gang together with seasonal arts and crafts, fish feedings, movie nights, and more. Tots will also love meeting the property’s flock of Chilean flamingos, practicing their putt-putt on the 18-hole miniature golf course, and ordering off the children’s menus available at all on-site dining outlets. Families can also hop aboard boats departing from the hotel lobby for a cruise along the resort’s waterways.

Location: Chicago, IllinoisPrice: From $129 per night

The Loews Loves Families initiative, available at 27 properties throughout North America, is one of the most baby-friendly hotel offerings around. Guest rooms are equipped with mini fridges and kettles for storing and sanitizing bottles; full-size cribs, baby tubs, and night-lights are complimentary. Housekeeping will cover electrical outlets and supply foam bumpers upon request, and kids are given a cute amenity kit with baby lotion, wipes, shampoo, conditioner, and body wash. Board games, coloring books, pool toys, and iPads preloaded with movies and games are available from the concierge desk, as is a family activity guide highlighting the best local options for museums, zoos, and kid-friendly restaurants. There’s even a Bedtime Book Cart to help parents maintain their routine while on the road.

Location: Sagres, PortugalPrice: From $149 per night

At Martinhal Sagres, a stylish beachfront resort tucked inside a protected natural park in Portugal’s Algarve, the littlest guests get the VIP treatment. A baby concierge stocks rooms with cribs, bottle sterilizers, high chairs, and other essentials before families arrive—sparing parents the frustration of hauling half the nursery overseas. Even better, the resort’s supervised kids clubs welcome infants as young as six months, with separate programs for crawling babies, curious toddlers, and older children. Accommodations range from contemporary hotel suites to spacious villas with kitchens and washing machines; other perks include five swimming pools, sandy playgrounds, and restaurants offering dedicated baby menus. The Baby's First Holiday package sweetens the deal with a couples massage and romantic dinner—babysitting included.

Location: Oklahoma City, OklahomaPrice: From $149 per night, inclusive of water park access for two people

Operated by the Chickasaw Nation, this 404-room property blends big-ticket family fun with a strong sense of place. When Julian and I visited, it was the cultural aspect that surprised us most—especially the Chickasaw-curated gallery and easy access to the Smithsonian-affiliated First Americans Museum next door, which recently debuted the fully immersive FAMily Discovery Center. Outside, the 4.5-acre lagoon complex boasts the fourth-largest pool in the country—complete with zip-line plunges, an inflatable obstacle course, and an adults-only swim-up bar for parents who need a moment of respite. Inside, the 100,000-square-foot water park is kept at a blissful 82 degrees and features a low tide pool with pint-sized splash structures that didn’t overwhelm my budding swimmer.

There’s an arcade, mirror maze, and candy store, plus a slew of specialty eateries serving the four main food groups for toddlers: hot dogs, pizza, ice cream, and tacos. On Friday and Saturday evenings, there’s even a storytelling Pajama Hour led by resort staff at the lobby fireplace, with bedtime attire encouraged. Families will appreciate the value here: Children under two stay free, and spacious suites offer bunk beds and semi-private sleeping areas, with cribs available on request.

Location: Puerto Morelos, MexicoPrice: From $420 per night

As far as resorts for families go, Sensira, an all-inclusive luxury resort on the Riviera Maya, sure knows how to make a kid feel special. The Baby Explorer Club, designed for ages 18 months through 3 years, has indoor slides, bounce houses, and a ball pit, plus supervised sensory activities, music, and storytelling. For families with older kids in tow, there’s a movie theater, miniature golf course, zip line, water park, basketball court, tennis court, climbing wall, gaming stations, indoor trampoline park, and two swimming pools (there's a third pool designated for adults only).

The hotel can prepare fresh purées on request for infants and toddlers and has a kids corner at the buffet with food displayed at little ones’ eye level. It also supplies all the equipment parents need for a hassle-free stay, including bottle warmers and sterilizers, full-size cribs, and car seats. Babysitting services are available from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. daily, and parents are given a beeper to stay in touch. (If an infant is still breastfeeding, the nanny will fetch a parent for mealtime.) Even the spa takes family well-being into consideration, offering a full slate of all-ages wellness programming, including gentle therapies for children and teens that mirror adult rituals, and purpose-built family treatment cabins.

Location: Crete, GreecePrice: From $199 per night

Phāea Cretan Malia is one of those rare design hotels that’s as thoughtfully geared toward families with babies and toddlers as it is toward style-hungry adults. The low-rise, modernist buildings sit in lush, shady gardens that keep the grounds cool even in peak summer heat. When Julian and I stayed here in 2024, we spent hours pinballing from the sandy, shallow beach to the swimming pools to the Tiny Explorers’ Club—a padded, sunlit playroom for ages three and under where parents can spend time with their little ones.

For ages 3–12, the Little Explorers Kids Club has its own kitchen for baking sessions, a mini stage for dance and theater, an environmental play area, an organic garden to tend, and an outdoor playground—a godsend when little ones have energy to burn. Parents can also request the Baby Package, available for an additional charge, which includes babysitting services and toddler gear to cut down on packing. And while the open-air restaurants serve gorgeous Cretan dishes built around local produce, they’re equally prepared for picky palates: think wood-fired pizzas, simple pastas, and fresh fruit. When you’re ready to venture out, Potamos Beach and the Minoan ruins of Malia Palace, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, are an easy walk away.

Location: Southern Kalahari, South AfricaPrice: From around $7,000 per night for two adults, all-inclusive

Taking a toddler on safari sounds like a terrible idea until you discover Tswalu, South Africa’s largest privately protected conservation area, in the malaria-free Kalahari. At Loapi, six stand-alone safari homes with one or two bedrooms have private plunge pools, chefs, house managers, and dedicated guides, trackers, and vehicles—meaning no one cares if your child talks incessantly through a lion sighting. (Mine certainly did.)

When we visited in August 2026, Julian raced our guide and tracker through the red dunes, dictated his pasta preferences to the chef, and played catch with his child minder while I squeezed in some work. The flexibility is extraordinary: Game drives can be tailored around naps and short attention spans while older siblings can learn archery and animal tracking through the Junior Ranger program. Other highlights include close-up encounters with habituated meerkats and some of the best stargazing I've experienced anywhere. We also spotted black-maned lions, cheetahs, wild dogs, and desert black rhinos, but some of Julian’s happiest moments were spent chasing a ball with the staff. For families seeking a (slightly) less extravagant safari, Tswalu’s Motse camp offers one- and two-bedroom suites and shared facilities; its five-bedroom Tarkuni homestead is another option for multigenerational groups of up to 10.

Location: Atami, Shizuoka Prefecture, JapanPrice: From $238 per night

Less than an hour by bullet train from Tokyo, Risonare Atami sits high above a Japanese seaside town famous for its hot springs and fireworks festivals. All 81 rooms overlook Sagami Bay, with some offering front-row views of the town’s fireworks displays. The resort’s Baby-Friendly Stay Plan outfits spacious rooms with cribs and other infant necessities, while the restaurants serve complimentary rice porridge and vegetable purées. Parents can even hand off children as young as six months to an in-house nursery for up to 150 minutes of complimentary childcare while they tuck into a multicourse kaiseki dinner at the hotel’s restaurant, Hanabi.

Little ones have a heated indoor pool with a shallow splash zone and an ocean-view playroom with a ball pit and toddler-friendly climbing wall. Outdoors, Kusu Kusu centers on a tree house built into a 300-year-old camphor tree, with forest treasure hunts for children ages two and up and a treetop obstacle course for older kids. Parents can also steal away to the resort's semi-open-air onsen overlooking the bay.

Location: Grossarl, AustriaPrice: From $669 per night, including full board and childcare

Part luxury Alpine retreat, part working organic farm, Moar Gut is a five-star family resort where children can feed goats, cuddle rabbits, and even “adopt” an animal to care for during their stay. Set on a sprawling car-free estate in Austria’s Grossarl Valley, the 46-suite property takes its back-to-nature philosophy seriously. Its 10,000-square-foot kids club is built from natural materials like wood, linen, and sheep’s wool, with a painting studio, woodworking workshops, and guided forest adventures. Even babies get the full Alpine treatment: The separate nursery, offering supervised care from 30 days old, has Swiss stone pine cribs, organic bedding, and hay-covered walls. At the Lillee Baby Spa, parents can book guided infant massage, yoga, or floating sessions starting at three weeks old. Older children can ride ponies, forage for alpine herbs, and bake traditional Austrian treats, while parents have an adults-only spa and six-course farm-to-table dinners to look forward to. There's even a dedicated organic baby buffet with fresh purées and formula.

What is the best destination to travel to with an infant and/or toddler?

For a first trip with a baby or toddler, destinations with manageable flight times, reliable medical care, and resorts that minimize the logistical headaches of traveling with little ones are ideal. Florida, Mexico, and the Caribbean are excellent starting points, with direct flights from many US cities, and resorts that cater specifically to young children. Four Seasons Resort and Residences Anguilla is one standout, offering complimentary baby equipment, a zero-entry family pool, and a splash pad. For families ready to venture farther, Portugal's Algarve is another excellent choice, especially Martinhal Sagres, where supervised childcare starts at six months. In the Austrian Alps, Moar Gut goes a step further, welcoming infants as young as 30 days into its professionally staffed nursery.

Are there any good all-inclusive resorts for infants and toddlers?

Absolutely. Jean-Michel Cousteau Resort in Fiji is particularly impressive, with meals, activities, and dedicated nanny care included in the rate. Children under six are assigned two nannies who work opposite shifts, providing personalized care throughout the day and evening, while older children are paired with Fijian companions who guide them through age-appropriate activities. Closer to home, Grand Velas Riviera Nayarit in Mexico features gourmet dining, a baby concierge who arranges infant equipment and coordinates meals and childcare, and specialty purées for its youngest guests (babysitting costs extra).

What resort in the US is best for families with infants and toddlers?

The Breakers Palm Beach in Florida is hard to beat. Its private beach and zero-entry family pool are ideal for little swimmers, while a 4,500-square-foot playground and the Seaside Family Entertainment Center—with its dedicated Toddler Cove—give youngsters room to burn off energy. The hotel can also supply cribs, strollers, and bottle warmers, as well as childproof guest rooms upon request. Parents, meanwhile, get the restaurants, spa, and old-school Palm Beach glamour that have made The Breakers a fixture on luxury travel lists for generations.

We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6530. The Sky Today on Friday, November 20: The Moon passes Saturn and Neptune

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M. EST; 12 hours later, our satellite passes 7° north of Saturn at 8 P.M. EST. The trio is visible in the southeastern sky two hours after sunset, forming a triangle with the Moon to the upper left of Saturn, and Neptune to Saturn’s right. Only the Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, while Neptune will require optical aid.

From the gibbous Moon, drop down first to check out Saturn through a telescope, including its lovely ring system and brightest moon, Titan. Saturn is the brightest object in this part of the sky after the Moon, so you don’t have to worry about misidentifying it. After passing south of the ringed world earlier this week, Titan now sits about 3.2’ to Saturn’s west, in line with the rings. Fainter moons Tethys, Rhea, and Dione may be visible clustered closer to the planet, but the bright moonlight might also make them challenging for visual observation.

From Saturn, scan 6.6° west-southwest to land on Neptune. If you have a go-to scope, it may take you right to the outermost planet, which glows at magnitude 7.7 and offers up a tiny, 2”-wide disk. It may look like a “flat,” bluish-gray star, rather than a bright pinprick of white light. Look for a large parallelogram of 4th- and 5th-magnitude stars just over 9° to Saturn’s southwest if you need a closer stepping stone. The star at the northeastern point of that shape is 5th-magnitude 29 Piscium, and it lies about 2.6° southwest of Neptune.

Sunrise: 6:51 A.M.Sunset: 4:40 P.M.Moonrise: 2:04 P.M.Moonset: 2:12 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (84%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

As NASA's Voyager 1 probe reaches one light-day from Earth, we look back at its legendary photos of Jupiter that changed our view of the solar system.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

This Wednesday (Nov. 18), humanity's most distant spacecraft will hit a new milestone. NASA's Voyager 1 probe, which has been exploring our solar system at increasingly remote depths since 1977, will reach 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth — a distance so vast, it takes light 24 hours to traverse the space between Voyager and our planet.

While we celebrate this achievement on Earth, Voyager 1 will observe its "light-day" in darkness; mission scientists turned off the probe's camera in 1990, immediately after it snapped its iconic "Pale Blue Dot" and "Solar System Family Portrait" images from beyond the orbit of Neptune. But before that, Voyager 1 had already taken tens of thousands of images of our cosmic neighborhood, and some of them totally transformed our understanding of the outer planets.

One of the most significant pieces of Voyager 1's legacy is its trip to Jupiter. From January to April 1979, the probe observed the solar system's largest planet and several of its giant moons up close, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As it approached, Voyager snapped a photo of the gas giant every 96 seconds to create this incredible time-lapse movie of Jupiter's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of a month in 1979.

Voyager observed discrete bands of Jupiter's atmosphere spinning at various speeds and in different directions, like a cosmic Rubik's Cube being twisted by an invisible hand. Clouds speed by as if on conveyor belts as giant, planet-size storms swirl.

Voyager's time-lapse film captures about 60 full days on Jupiter — the equivalent of about a month on Earth, since each Jupiter day is roughly 10 Earth hours —- providing the most comprehensive and high-resolution look at the planet yet. The observations significantly built on the data captured by NASA's Pioneer 10 and 11 Jupiter probes, which launched half a decade prior, showing the planet's atmosphere to be much more dynamic than astronomers realized.

Just before making its closest approach to the planet, Voyager spotted something remarkable: Jupiter had a thin, faint ring system. Made primarily of dust, the rings appeared only when Voyager saw Jupiter backlit by the sun. No telescope had ever seen this before, but ground-based observatories soon confirmed the rings' existence, and Voyager 2 took even clearer pictures of the rings when it reached Jupiter in July 1979.

Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring of dust around Jupiter when it was backlit by the sun.

We now know that all four outer planets — Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — have rings. Today, scientists suspect Jupiter's dusty rings are replenished partially by volcanic eruptions on the planet's volatile moon Io.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This discovery, too, can be linked to Voyager. While making a close approach to Io, the spacecraft witnessed the first-ever volcanic eruption on a world beyond Earth. This observation showed that moons, not just planets, can be geologically active. In this image, a giant volcano called Loki Patera (the largest volcano on Io, measuring an estimated 125 miles, or 200 km, wide) spews its guts into space.

Voyager 1 witnessed a volcanic eruption (blue) on Io — the first volcaic eruption seen beyond Earth.

Taken together, these observations of Jupiter and its moons showed the largest planet and its moons to be a far more dynamic, complicated and chaotic system than anyone had realized. Moreover, the close-up views of these distant worlds made them more than just dots in the sky. It made them fully realized worlds — places to explore, map and eventually visit. Just this week, China's space agency announced its intention to send a lander to Jupiter's moon Callisto in the first-ever landing mission to the Jovian system.

Voyager 1's work continues in interstellar space, which it officially reached in 2012. With its camera off, it studies the radiation environment of space using magnetic field and plasma detectors — the last two of its 10 science instruments still receiving power. Scientists suspect the legendary probe will fully run out of power in the 2030s.

For more stunning space photos, check out our Space Photo of the Week gallery.

Brandon is the space / physics editor at Live Science. He holds a bachelor's degree in creative writing from the University of Arizona, with minors in journalism and media arts. His interests include black holes, asteroids and comets, and the search for extraterrestrial life.

#6526. As Democrats look to next era, the veto and the filibuster await

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer greets House Minority Whip Katherine Clark at the Center for American Progress Action Fund’s “Results to Roadmap” event on Thursday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

As Democrats continue their victory lap after their big wins on election night, outside groups and incoming freshmen are already turning up the pressure — and laying out competing visions of what the next two years should look like.

For Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, it bears repeating that “the Democrats aren’t all exactly the same.”

“The most important lesson of this whole election, and one we all need to internalize if we’re going to truly build a durable majority, is populism and moderation are not mutually exclusive,” he said at a Center for American Progress Action Fund event on Thursday.

Voters are expecting results as Democrats claim a mandate to address costs and corruption. “Our majority will be measured against one test and one test only: Have we made your life better?” Schumer said.

He acknowledged, however, that their plans could run into a President Donald Trump-sized wall: the presidential veto.

“Will everything pass? Will Trump sign all of it into law? Knowing Trump’s and Republicans’  intransigence, of course not. But I will promise the American people: The Democratic Party will fight to make your life more affordable, your government more competent, your capital less corrupt, bill by bill, brick by brick, for as long as it takes for you to feel the difference,” Schumer said, hinting the road could be a long one.

But several progressive lawmakers and groups say the next Congress cannot be business as usual.

Indivisible, a progressive political organization that has described the Trump administration as a “fascistic clown show,” sent a memo to Senate Democratic offices Thursday morning urging them not to “squander” their momentum and to “fight at a level that matches the public’s demand for action.”

“Who leads the party in this era must be an open question, not a coronation. It’s time to define what the next era of the Democratic Party will be,” the memo reads.

The group has been encouraging voters to speak up and demand their senators hold “a contested leadership election, not a cleared field for Schumer.”

Meanwhile, Schumer has projected confidence he will keep his spot atop the caucus, especially after he helped pave the way for Tuesday’s blue wave. “I’ll be reelected as majority leader,” he said Wednesday. But the pressure campaign points to some tough math and harsh realities for the top Democrat — including some that mirror the woes of the outgoing Republican Majority Leader John Thune.

Among the demands outlined by Indivisible is one with a troubled recent history: “Breaking the filibuster on the first day of the new session.”

Democrats need to leverage “every procedural tool” if they “want the public to believe their campaign promises weren’t just more talk from politicians who are just like the old politicians they hated,” the memo reads.

The group isn’t alone in floating a new approach to the chamber’s 60-vote threshold for invoking cloture and ending debate. Some current and incoming lawmakers have signaled they would be open to going “nuclear” and abolishing the legislative filibuster, following in the footsteps of past majorities in both parties who have similarly changed how other Senate business is handled, like judicial nominees.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., argued in an op-ed in Time this week that Democrats could in some cases use existing tools, like a party-line process known as budget reconciliation, to pass their priorities. For non-budget items, like “bills to ban stock trading by federal officials or crack down on Trump’s corruption in plain sight,” Democrats should start by putting them up for a vote on the floor and letting “Republicans decide if they want to stay tied to such corruption.”

“And, if they do, then let’s clear away Senate filibuster rules and pass the laws anyway,” she wrote.

Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas told NBC News on Monday ahead of his victory, “I believe the majority has the right to govern in this country, and the filibuster, which is not in the Constitution and is a Jim Crow relic, is leading to gridlock in our nation’s capital.”

Schumer ignored a question about nuking the filibuster at Wednesday’s event, saying instead, “The first thing we’ll do is reduce costs and work the legislative process.”

It would take 51 votes in the Senate for Democrats to go “nuclear” and establish a new precedent, a math problem that Thune knows all too well. The Republican from South Dakota faced loud criticism from conservatives online and hard-liners in his own party who said he wasn’t doing enough to try to pass a sprawling voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act. But Thune repeatedly insisted he didn’t have the votes to change the chamber’s filibuster rules.

Many senators fear that blowing up the 60-vote threshold would fundamentally change the role of the Senate and its ability to tap the brakes on legislation that doesn’t have durable bipartisan support. Democrats went through a similar debate over the filibuster in 2022, during Schumer's first stint as majority leader. Even as others in their party pushed to pass sweeping voting rights legislation by any means necessary, Kyrsten Sinema and Joe Manchin, then moderate Democratic senators, held firm against filibuster changes.

And Schumer will have at least one Democrat on his hands who has already spoken up in defense of the filibuster, reversing his previous position. “I now recognize how important the filibuster is and the state our country would be in without it,” Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania wrote in a Washington Post op-ed earlier this summer, praising Sinema and Manchin as “courageous” holdouts who were wrongly “vilified” for holding the line.

None of that points to an easy ride for the incoming Democratic majority leader. And if fights over the filibuster weren’t enough, the caucus is also bracing for a different kind of intraparty angst, this time over impeachment.

The next likely House Judiciary Committee chairman, Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., told reporters on Thursday: “I have not had a single member of Congress or even a candidate say we’ve got to start out by impeaching Donald Trump.”

“For us, impeachment is not a fetish. It’s certainly not a taboo. We’ve impeached the guy twice,” he said, referring to Democrats’ efforts during the first Trump administration. “The problem has been over on the Senate side, and for us, it is a tool in the constitutional toolkit.”

Even if the House were to impeach Trump, a conviction would require a two-thirds supermajority vote in the Senate. And some Democrats are eager not to waste their hard-earned political capital on an impeachment quest that could alienate moderate voters and do nothing to bring down costs for everyday Americans.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who boosted candidates in battleground races and recently released a roadmap for the new Congress, said at the CAP event on Thursday that lawmakers should “hold oversight hearings and expose the corruption of this administration. I’m not suggesting that that necessarily leads to impeachment. Maybe it does.”

Sounding more certain for Democrats in both chambers is their desire to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran.

But that could be dealt with in the lame duck if Rep. Thomas Massie’s, R-Ky., resolution prevails next week. His proposal includes eight articles of impeachment, including allegations that Hegseth violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Hegseth said in a video on Thursday of impeaching: “Didn’t work against President Trump. Won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”

Indivisible’s memo names impeaching Hegseth as a priority, as well as blocking a “business-as-usual” National Defense Authorization Act in the lame duck and refusing to fund the Department of Defense if “it doesn’t cut off money for the war.”

But it’s not clear that Democrats in Congress are ready to play that kind of hard ball. As they weigh their approach to the next era, they’re still half-stunned themselves by their larger than expected wins — and trying to put themselves in the best position ahead of the next elections in 2028.

GOP Rep. Christopher H. Smith of New Jersey told reporters on Thursday at the Capitol he hopes Democrats don’t hold up the NDAA “for the good of the country.”

“The NDAA is such an important bill for our national security, and it’s usually very bipartisan. I hope it is,” he said.

John Donnelly and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#6524. Inside NYC’s Pool Scene, the City’s Great Equalizer

Just when we thought New York had seen it all, I caught wind that the first-ever five-borough pool tournament—in the city’s history—was about to kick off.

It was all thanks to Dan Tran, the brains behind the Five Boro Break. Tran has been shooting pool across the city for more than a decade and has played on more than 130 tables out of the 400 to 500 he estimates are in NYC (he even catalogs them out of his own goodwill for other New Yorkers, on Pool Tables NYC). He’s just that guy: an absolute force of nature with a heavy case of do-the-impossible syndrome. One day over summer, at a league night with fellow pool-playing regulars, he wondered if there was a way to get folks like these together for one big game—to unite New York’s pool-playing dive bar families and play as one.

Dan Tran, the brains behind the Five Boro Break, has been shooting pool across the city for more than a decade.

The idea was a tournament “built by pool players, run by pool players,” says Tran, who you’ll most often find playing at George & Jacks in Williamsburg. “No money changing hands, no ulterior motive.” Just bringing together this community, which Tran is the first to admit existed long before he stepped on the scene.

So this powerhouse did it: 256 players, 16 venues, all five boroughs, over two days in early November. When I caught up with Tran the week before the tournament, he still couldn’t believe he was bringing the idea to life. “I was like, 'What am I signing up to do once I post this?' But then I posted it, and it just took off—like completely took off. And everybody was like, 'Yeah, we can totally do this.'”

Entry was set at just $25, and anyone could sign up once the link went live. Volunteers were coordinated to run the tournament at each of the 16 bars, and local businesses chipped in more than $6,000 in giveaways. The grand prize: a custom street sign from the New York City Department of Transportation reading “Five Boro Break Champion."

I rode the wave of Tran’s infectious energy and spent an entire weekend hopping between dives watching the tournament’s pool players do what they do best.

The audience at NYC bar Sugar Mouse applauds Five Boro Break creator Dan Tran at the finals.

On Saturday, November 7, you could feel it in the air. There was something electric about knowing the grittiest corners of New York City were locked in on the same game. That distinct four o’clock autumn sunlight was shining on Bushwick Ice House, one of the 16 venues, when I walked in with Traveler’s Julia Abbonizio and Skyli Alvarez, who were ready to photograph the scene. Gathered around a red-felt table were a dozen or so players who shot us “what’s up” nods as we entered; the bartender moseyed over with “what’s it gonna be?” eyes. Without a word exchanged, we were already part of the bar’s family.

The crowd around us was dressed in their dive-bar best (jeans), and glowing under the neon-red Budweiser lights. The energy in the room matched the game unfolding. One moment, the place roared with Miller High Life clinks and friends catching up. The next it would go pin-drop silent as someone bent over and lined up a shot. More often than not, we’d hear a “nice” before the cue even struck, or a congratulatory clap before someone sank the 8-ball, because everyone knew the game well enough to see exactly what was coming.

Will Pay, a Bushwick Ice House regular, designed the tournament's felt-green shirts.

Satoe Onizuka plays Netta Rawner (left) at Bushwick Ice House.

Will Pay, a Bushwick resident and the creative mind behind the tournament’s T-shirt and site design—dark green, like a pool table’s felt, and featuring a solid orange 5-ball to nod to the boroughs—was running the show. He jokingly told me he’s something of a pool scout around the city, sniffing out the best shooters to join his league. Pay attested that, when Tran initially announced the tournament, interest at his local dive Bushwick Ice House was immediate. Within 10 minutes of the link being live, the waitlist to play at the venue had passed 100.

While Satoe Onizuka, the stealthiest star of the regulars, shook another hand after winning yet another round, I snuck outside of Bushwick Ice House to chat with Pay, who was wearing the Five Boro Break shirt he designed. We got into the type of conversation you do at a dive bar or around a pool table. The love of the game. The importance of dives as sacred spaces. The alluring seediness of it all. Pay knows how we got here: “The game itself is called billiards, but it got casualized to ‘pool’ because people used to throw a ton of money on the table—pool their money—and gamble,” Pay said. “Obviously, that’s gone out the window because everyone’s super chill these days, but what’s cool is that it still has that air of danger, of being something a bit forbidden.” Will’s right: it’s never corny to shoot pool. No matter who you are, it makes you feel like the slickest person in the room.

There’s also that sense that you’re part of something bigger. Back inside, Pay gestured around the room. “Look at this place,” he said in admiration. “There’s literally no real estate for this table. But it’s here. And without it, this place would simply not be what it is. These people would probably not be here in this bar. I don’t even think this bar would exist.”

The enthusiasm at Bushwick Ice House reminded me of how this tournament could only have happened because NYC dive bars already operate as tight-knit communities of their own. They’re the ultimate third places, the spots that aren’t home or work—and the pool table is, in fact, their beating heart.

By 9 p.m. on Saturday, when we stumbled into LES’ Sadie’s Ward, '80s dance-pop shook the walls. Drinks were flowing, the room glowed disco-lit, and everyone was having such a good time you had to shout to be heard by the person next to you. A group of hodge-podge regulars stood two and three deep around the pool table, watching the small, curly-haired Amanda Andries, one of the bar’s most beloved shooters, sink her way toward Sunday’s finals.

Andries is one of the Ladies of Sadie’s, a magnetic group of female regulars at this bar, who were gassing each other up and out-shooting all the 6-foot-something men in flannels that dared to play them. For all the history that tables at bars like Sadie’s have absorbed, it’s the people gathered around them who make the pool scene so captivating—and at this bar, the social fabric is very tightly knit.

East Williamsburg's Anchored Inn was one of the 16 bars that hosted Five Boro Break games.

We sat in the small hideaway across from the bar as the games rolled on, reflecting on the players we’d met throughout the tournament so far: soft-spoken, sharp-shooting Audrey Jones at Anchored Inn over loaded Carmen fries; Allegra “Legz” Fierro outside the graffied, mirrorless bathroom at Blue Ruin Bar; and Elvin Estevez, a polite killer on the table, in the leather booths at Twins Lounge. I’d asked each to tell me their golden rule of playing pool in this city, but it all came back to one recurring theme: be a good person. There’s a camaraderie in wanting to keep NYC’s pool scene a sacred place.

It’s easy not to suck, though. Sam Shumway of Pool Table Archive said to me by phone in the days following the event. Five years ago, he started posting photos of the pool tables he’d played on in cities across the US, but his hobby grew into a living record of pool culture.

“Pool tables are special because they’re a snapshot of a time and a place in a bar,” he told me. “A lot of these tables are older than you are. Like, that’s a 40-year-old table. Imagine how much life it’s seen around it.” You can picture a montage of scenes immediately: 4 a.m. closings, birthday toasts, new friendships, awkward first dates, breakups, and more than a few questionable decisions. Maybe a win in the first-ever cross-city tournament.

Allegra “Legz” Fierro in Hell's Kitchen's Blue Ruin Bar, just before a match

Come Sunday, we walked into a jam-packed, purple-lit Sugar Mouse for the finals. The winners from each of the 16 bars would go head-to-head across two pool tables. A live dad rock band jammed in the corner, and all I saw were familiar faces from Saturday’s hijinks, smiling, watching respectfully, nodding when a friend nailed a shot, and hugging and shaking hands when one missed. As the field dwindled to four semifinalists, then just two, the crowd drew tighter around the remaining table. Two large projectors cast a live feed onto the wall, as former WPBA No. 1 Jennifer Barretta commented and Hall of Famer John Leyman refereed with a stern eye.

We were all there for the moment Brennan Brooks of the BCA Brooklyn Travel League took the inaugural win, cementing his right to take home that iconic sign. But as I took in the room around me, what stood out most was seeing people packed in like sardines to watch their fellow dive bar regulars take the stage. It was a kaleidoscope of communities, each representing their local with love. The Five Boro Break was never just about winning; it was about creating a space where everyone could be part of something.

A triumphant moment at Sadie's Ward on the Lower East Side

The East Village's Sugar Mouse hosted the tournament final.

It was a fresh alternative to life on a screen—maybe that’s part of why so many people showed up. “People are craving human connection again; people are craving something to do with their hands,” Shumway had said. And though it might look too cool, or intimidating, everyone has a place if they want it. “Pool brings together people who would normally have nothing in common. And there are no pre-qualifications for putting your name on a chalkboard. You might get beat, and that’s okay.”

At the end of the Finals night, all of us riding a collective high, Tran stood next to the championship table to thank everyone who helped bring his vision to life. He couldn’t get a word out before the room burst into applause. Thirty seconds of it, and it showed no signs of letting up. Humble as he is, he just smiled.

Tran rattled off the bars, businesses, and people who stepped up to make the tournament possible, shaking his head happily. “This is what pool does,” he said. “It brings people together rather than pushes people apart.”

Or as Shumway likes to put it: “Pool is the great equalizer.”

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.
